mil5.2.8:1.2: ‘The Tathāgata has an inseparable assembly.’ And yet you also say:
mil5.2.8:1.3: ‘Five hundred bhikkhus were split away at a single stroke by Devadatta.’
mil5.2.8:1.4: If, Venerable Nāgasena, the Tathāgata has an inseparable assembly, then the statement that Devadatta split away five hundred bhikkhus at a single stroke is false.
mil5.2.8:1.5: And if Devadatta split away five hundred bhikkhus at a single stroke, then the statement ‘The Tathāgata has an inseparable assembly’ is also false.
mil5.2.8:1.6: This too is a two-horned dilemma that has come to you, profound, hard to untie, a knot even tighter than a knot. On this the people here are enveloped, shut in, hemmed in, covered over, and wrapped round. Show here the power of your wisdom against the doctrines of opponents.”
mil5.2.8:2.1: “Your majesty, the Tathāgata does have an inseparable assembly, and Devadatta did split away five hundred bhikkhus at a single stroke. But that was through the power of the one who causes the split. When one who causes a split is present, your majesty, there is nothing that is inseparable.
mil5.2.8:2.2: Where there is a splitter, a mother is divided from her son, and a son from his mother; a father from his son, and a son from his father; a brother from his sister, and a sister from her brother; a friend from his friend. A boat made of timbers joined together is broken by the force of a striking wave. A tree laden with sweet fruit is broken by the force of the wind. Even fine gold is cut by iron.
mil5.2.8:2.3: But, your majesty, that ‘the Tathāgata has a breakable assembly’ is not the intention of the wise, not the conviction of the Buddhas, not the wish of the learned.
mil5.2.8:2.4: And there is a reason here why the Tathāgata is called ‘one with an inseparable assembly.’
mil5.2.8:2.6: It has never been heard, your majesty, that the Tathāgata’s assembly was split because of anything he himself did, whether through not giving, unkind speech, harmful conduct, or lack of impartiality, in whatever way he conducted himself. For that reason the Tathāgata is called ‘one with an inseparable assembly.’
mil5.2.8:2.7: Do you know, your majesty, of anything in the Buddha’s word in its nine divisions, handed down in the suttas, saying ‘Because of this deed done by the Bodhisatta, the Tathāgata’s assembly was split’?”
mil5.2.8:2.8: “There is nothing, venerable sir. It is neither seen nor heard of in the world.
mil5.2.8:2.9: Well said, Venerable Nāgasena; it is so, and I accept it.”
